author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a plain five-step flow from start to finish, defines every term an outsider needs (rolling deploy, maxUnavailable, version id), gives a map of which steps do what, and explains why things happen in this order ("why the old key waited until now", "why readiness is gated"), so it is easier to follow cold; B covers more ground (staging drills, a 401 retry path, suspend before delete) but is denser and asks more of a newcomer.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A starts by explaining how the app runs: the snapshot, per-request reads, the 401 retry rule and a code example. It ends with a table of failure cases. That gives a newcomer a precise picture of the system before the rollout steps, while Document B leaves the runtime behaviour for the end and describes it less exactly.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a newcomer a clearer picture of how the system runs: separate sequence diagrams show every component (client, API, Postgres, worker, provider), a token lifecycle state diagram shows how a link moves between states, the worker has its own section, and a single live-link test is reused throughout; B explains its reasoning well up front but puts everything into one long linear diagram and never shows the token states as a picture.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it opens with what the change adds (one table, three endpoints, one page, two emails), splits the design into separate request, click/submit and worker sections, gives each a sequence diagram with all the actors and its own "why it is built this way" notes, draws the token lifecycle as a state diagram, and has a failure table with a "what the user sees" column, while A puts every flow into one long diagram that is thorough but harder to read.

author: sonnet
reason: I'd rather be handed B, though it's close. It describes the existing system in its own plain paragraph before the new design. Its tables for stored data and failures are easy to scan. It names the generic reply [G] and the expired page [E] so they don't have to be repeated, and it explains its choices, such as why a GET must not use up the token. A covers about as much, but it mixes existing-system facts into a long glossary and packs the rest into denser prose.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the same design in a tighter, easier order: it starts with the existing system, defines short labels ([G], [E]) that the diagram uses, and gives the schema and the failure cases their own tables, while B packs its failure paths into the diagram block and spreads the explanation across long notes.

author: haiku
reason: A suits a reader who does not know the stack: it defines Redis, Postgres, OpenID Connect, GETDEL and bcrypt, and it covers race and database-error paths, the retry and why it chose each assumption. B gives a sharper four-outcome overview and better reasoning for asking for the password, but it assumes the reader already knows OIDC and Redis, and its "starts from step N" cross-references are slightly off.

author: haiku
reason: Document A opens with the whole picture: the four outcomes and the key security reason (a verified Google email does not prove ownership of our account, so the password is required). After that, its flowchart, steps and tables stay tight and say exactly what state changes. B adds useful endpoint names and term definitions, but it is longer and more repetitive, refers to an unseen "brief", and in places says "nothing changes" when the flow record has already been used up.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because its flowchart is split into numbered, colour-coded sections that match the step list, it explains basics like OIDC, PKCE and JWKS, and it gives reasons for its choices (why a password is needed, why the login start needs no CSRF), while A's single large diagram is harder to read even though A explains the existing lockout and reset mechanics more fully.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the existing system a newcomer needs (the lockout rules, POST /forgot, a shared check_password_with_lockout, why a confirm token replaces CSRF) and adds an endpoints table plus the reason behind each decision, so it is easier to follow end to end, even though A is tighter and has a cleaner colour-coded diagram.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer and denser, but it explains every step the same way (what starts it, what it does, what data it keeps, how it fails) and gives the reasons behind its choices, such as using the replay-timestamp cutoff and a conditional-write lock; B is easier to read but leaves real gaps open, including how manual reruns and Sunday reloads avoid colliding with the nightly run, hung attempts, and a serving table named `orders` like the source table.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier to follow for a newcomer: it gives a short, consistent flow (controller, attempts, one commit transaction, 06:00 check, Sunday reconciliation), a clean diagram and a clear failure table, and it says plainly where it leaves gaps. B covers more edge cases, but its lock, timeout races, replay-timestamp cutoff and awkward step ordering (step 7 "starts when step 8 opens") make the core mechanism harder to pick out.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a summary and explicit "why it is shaped this way" rationale, gives the diagram a legend, and numbers the steps so the diagram, the step-by-step prose and the trigger table line up; A packs the same mechanics into a denser opening paragraph and a busier flowchart that are harder to orient from cold.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to learn the system from: its summary walks through the main flow and then says why each design choice was made, its diagram has a legend and numbered steps that match the step-by-step text, and its sections are clearly split up; B covers some extra edge cases (crash after commit, replica replay lag) but opens with one dense paragraph and its diagram is harder to follow.
